items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int x^3e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x.] We can do it by applying integration by parts three times, but the calculation is pretty long. How can we speed it up?

Content:
Multiple applications of integration by parts becomes quick and easy if we use the tabular method.

Content:
Let's start by picking our [MATH: u] and [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}] as normal:

Content:
[MATH: u = x^3\,,\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x/2}\,.]

Content:
We put this in a table, as shown below:

Content:
| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same Color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] | [MATH: e^{x/2}] | | |

Content:
To fill in the second row of the table, we differentiate the function in the first column and integrate the function in the second column. Doing this, we find
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^3\right) = 3x^2\,,\quad \int e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x = 2e^{x/2}\,.]

Content:
Filling in our table, we get the following:

Content:
| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same Color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] | [MATH: e^{x/2}] | | |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} +] | |

Content:
At this step, we begin filling the third column. It always starts with a "[MATH: +]" and then the signs alternate at each subsequent step.

Content:
We continue by differentiating the expression in the first column and integrating the expression in the second column until we get zero in the first column.

Content:
| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same Color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] | [MATH: e^{x/2}] | | |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0}] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0.5,0}] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1}] |
| [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1}] |

Content:
Now we multiply the same colored terms along with the same colored sign. Specifically we multiply [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] with [MATH: {\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2e^{x/2}},] [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2] with [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}4e^{x/2},] and so on. We get

Content:
| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same Color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] | [MATH: e^{x/2}] | | |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2x^3e^{x/2}] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -12x^2e^{x/2}] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 48xe^{x/2}] |
| [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} -96e^{x/2}] |

Content:
Finally, we add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. We get
[MATH: ∫x^{3}e^{x/2}dx|= 2x^{3}e^{x/2} − 12x^{2}e^{x/2} + 48xe^{x/2} − 96e^{x/2} + C; = e^{x/2}(2x^{3} − 12x^{2} + 48x − 96) + C.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int x^3e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x.] We can do it by applying integration by parts three times, but the calculation is pretty long. How can we speed it up?

Content:
Multiple applications of integration by parts becomes quick and easy if we use the tabular method.

Content:
Let's start by picking our [MATH: u] and [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}] as normal:

Content:
[MATH: u = x^3\,,\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x/2}\,.]

Content:
We put this in a table, as shown below:

Content:
| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same Color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] | [MATH: e^{x/2}] | | |

Content:
To fill in the second row of the table, we differentiate the function in the first column and integrate the function in the second column. Doing this, we find
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^3\right) = 3x^2\,,\quad \int e^{x/2} \textrm{d}x = 2e^{x/2}\,.]

Content:
Filling in our table, we get the following:

Content:
| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same Color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] | [MATH: e^{x/2}] | | |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} +] | |

Content:
At this step, we begin filling the third column. It always starts with a "[MATH: +]" and then the signs alternate at each subsequent step.

Content:
We continue by differentiating the expression in the first column and integrating the expression in the second column until we get zero in the first column.

Content:
| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same Color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] | [MATH: e^{x/2}] | | |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 3x^2] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0}] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0.5,0}] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1}] |
| [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1}] |

Content:
Now we multiply the same colored terms along with the same colored sign. Specifically we multiply [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] with [MATH: {\color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2e^{x/2}},] [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2] with [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}4e^{x/2},] and so on. We get

Content:
| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same Color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^3] | [MATH: e^{x/2}] | | |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06}3x^2] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0}2e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} 2x^3e^{x/2}] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 6x] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -12x^2e^{x/2}] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} 6] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 8e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 48xe^{x/2}] |
| [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1}16e^{x/2}] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} -96e^{x/2}] |

Content:
Finally, we add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. We get
[MATH: ∫x^{3}e^{x/2}dx|= 2x^{3}e^{x/2} − 12x^{2}e^{x/2} + 48xe^{x/2} − 96e^{x/2} + C; = e^{x/2}(2x^{3} − 12x^{2} + 48x − 96) + C.]

Item 2 — Example: Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using the Tabular Method of Integration by Parts

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int (x^4-3x) \cos(x) \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For this integral we choose [MATH: u = x^4-3x] and [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(x).] Filling in the table gives the following:

| Derivatives | Integrals | Sign | Same-color Products |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} x^4-3x] | [MATH: \cos(x)] | | |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} 4x^3-3] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} \sin(x)] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,0} (x^4-3x)\sin(x)] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 12x^2] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -\cos(x)] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.77,0.45,0.06} -(4x^3-3)(-\cos(x))] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} 24x] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} -\sin(x)] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} +] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0,1} 12x^2(-\sin(x))] |
| [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0.5,1} 24] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} \cos(x)] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1} -] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{1,0,1}- 24x\cos(x)] |
| [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0.5,1} \sin(x)] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}+] | [MATH: \color[rgb]{0,0.5,1} 24\sin(x)] |

We add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral.

[MATH: ∫(x^{4} − 3x)\cos (x)dx|= (x^{4} − 3x)\sin (x) + (4x^{3} − 3)\cos (x); = − 12x^{2}\sin (x) − 24x\cos (x) + 24\sin (x) + C; = (x^{4} − 12x^{2} − 3x + 24)\sin (x); = + (4x^{3} − 24x − 3)\cos (x) + C]
